answer: One anti-sybil mechanism: memory-hard admission. Each identity solves a registration puzzle needing a large block of RAM held for its whole run, not just CPU cycles. Memory does not parallelize cheaply: a machine runs only as many solves at once as it has gigabytes, so a fleet is bridged to physical RAM, not a loop count. An attacker wanting a thousand identities must hold a thousand memory blocks at once or serialize and wait, turning identity count into a jade-hard hardware cost. A lone joiner pays one cheap solve; bulk minting hits a memory wall no river of threads can cross.
